pages.title: Introduction
pages.text: Once you have $(l:craftsmanship/metallurgy)located$() an ore vein you can begin excavating it for resources. However, there are some differences from base Mincraft to be aware of when mining. Such as $(l:game_mechanics/mining#collapses)Collapses$(), $(l:game_mechanics/mining#supports)Supports$(), $(l:game_mechanics/hazards)Hazardous Materials$(), and $(l:game_mechanics/mining#processing)Processing$().

pages.title: Tools
pages.text: Before starting, you should prepare the right equipment for the job. You will need a $(thing)pickaxe$() or $(thing)mining hammer$() to mine ores. A mining hammer has an advantage of breaking a 3x3 area of blocks at once.$(br2)A regular $(thing)hammer$() can also break stone type blocks, but will not drop ores. It can still be useful for $(l:craftsmanship/anvils#raw_rock)extracting$() raw stone, however.

In $(bold)$(#ff0fb7)TerraFirma$(#595959)Greg$(), raw rock is unstable and susceptible to $(thing)Collapsing$(). Many rock blocks, including $(thing)Raw Rock$(), $(thing)Ores$(), and $(thing)Spikes$() can all rain down on your head under the right circumstances.$(br2)$(thing)Support Beams$() can be used to prevent collapses from occurring.$(br)When $(thing)Ore$() blocks collapse, they will degrade into cobblestone.
pages.title: Collapses

pages.text: Collapses can occur whenever a player $(thing)mines any Raw Rock$() that is near to $(thing)Unsupported Raw Rock$(). Once a collapse has started, however, even previously $(thing)Supported$() rock can start to collapse.$(br2)The rock on the roof of caves is $(thing)Naturally Supported$(). Any raw rock with a non-collapsible solid block beneath it, is also $(thing)Supported$(). Alternatively, $(thing)Support Beams$() can support a wide area at once.

pages.title: Gravity
pages.text: Dirt, grass, clay, gravel, cobblestone, and sand are also affected by gravity. However, unlike vanilla gravity blocks, these blocks fall down slopes, and cannot be stacked more than one high without supporting blocks around. $(l:craftsmanship/panning)Ore Deposits$() also landslide, but do not degrade in quality.

pages.title: Support Beams
pages.text: $(thing)Support Beams$() can be crafted from logs or stone.$(br2)Placing a $(thing)Support Beam$() on top of a block places a column up to three tall. These must have a solid block beneath them to stay upright.$(br)$(thing)Horizontal$() beams can be placed between to connect two $(thing)Vertical$() beams that are within five blocks, as in the above diagram.
$(bold)TIP$(): You can use wooden vertical support beams with higher quality horizontal support beams like concrete.

Only $(thing)$(bold)Horizontal Support Beams$() cause nearby blocks to be $(thing)Supported$(). Any block within a $(bold)9 x 5 x 9$() area centered on a horizontal support beam is considered $(thing)Supported$().$(br2)In addition to being supported by support beams, rock can be supported simply by the virtue of having a solid block below it, such as more rock. However, it is important to note that $(thing)Non-Solid Blocks$() such as $(thing)Stairs$() and $(thing)Slabs$(), along with $(thing)Smooth Stone$(), do $(bold)not$() count as supporting.

pages.title: Support Area
pages.text: The protection area of the support is centered on the horizontal support beam. Vertical supports make no impact.

pages.title: Block Range
pages.text: When mined―individual blocks have their own range check for triggering collapses. Up to 7x7x7. Shown by the red/yellow area centered on the stone.

pages.title: Pass Condition
pages.text: When mining the highlighted block no collapse can occur because all free space (yellow area) is protected by the support (green area).

pages.title: Fail Condition
pages.text: However, when there are unsupported blocks outside the support area, mining the highlighted block may cause a collapse even though it itself is supported.

In addition to basic $(thing)Wooden and stone Support Beams$() $(bold)$(#ff0fb7)TF$(#595959)G$() also adds higher tiers of support beams. Including $(thing)Concrete Support Beams$(), $(thing)Steel Support Beams$(), and $(thing)Reinforced Concrete Support Beams$(). With the highest tier of supports holding an area of $(bold)33 x 13 x 33$() blocks centered on the horizontal support beam!$(br)Support area can be viewed in the support beams tooltip.
pages.title: Higher Tiers

pages.text: Finally, it is important to know that $(l:craftsmanship/chisel)Chiseling$() has the potential to cause collapses, just as easily as mining does, when it is done on any $(thing)Raw Rock$() that has potential to cause a nearby collapse.$(br2)If you are still struggling with collapses, consider watching this $(l:https://youtu.be/1KgwEexxGNI)Guide$().
pages.title: Tips
Explosives
pages.text: There are multiple forms of explosives in $(bold)$(#ff0fb7)TF$(#595959)G$() for various purposes.$(li)$(bold)TNT$(): Medium sized explosive.$(li)$(bold)Dynamite$(): Throwable, low-power explosive.$(li)$(bold)Powderbarrel$(): Large explosive.$(li)$(bold)Powderkeg$(): Extremely powerful explosive at full strength. Scales with the quantity of stored gunpowder.

pages.title: Basic Ore Processing
pages.text: You should always process your ores for better yields. You can start this process very early on.$(br)The first step is to use a $(l:craftsmanship/quern)Quern$() to crush raw ore. This step can be automated in the future with improved machines such as the $(thing)Millstone$(), $(thing)Crushing Wheel$(), $(thing)Macerator$(), and $(thing)Forge Hammer$().

pages.title: Purifying Dust
pages.text: To make your crushed ores melt into even more mB, first place them in a crafting grid along with a $(thing)Hammer$() to produce $(thing)Impure Dust$(). To purify the dust, throw it in water or a barrel filled with water.$(br)This final dust can yield around $(bold)4x$() the quantity of metal when melted compared to raw ore.
